short_summary: US President Donald Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, but Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy noted the deal was unexpected while demanding reciprocal Russian commitments.

sources.name: The Guardian
sources.title: Trump announces partial ceasefire in Ukraine war as Zelenskyy says deal is ‘news to me’

sources.name: CNBC
sources.title: Trump declares 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine; Zelenskyy is waiting for details

paragraphs: A public diplomatic breach has erupted between Washington and Kyiv after US President Donald Trump unilaterally declared an energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine. Writing on Truth Social, Trump proclaimed that both belligerents had agreed to an immediate halt in long-range strikes against energy infrastructure, urging both parties not to break the alleged agreement. However, the announcement caught Ukrainian officials entirely off guard. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy revealed that the alleged deal was news to him, while reiterating that Ukraine remains open to a reciprocal cessation of strikes if Moscow halts its own devastating attacks on Ukrainian power grids and energy facilities.

The surprising declaration follows days of escalating friction between the White House and Kyiv. Tensions surged after Trump announced the lifting of US sanctions on Russian diesel exports, a policy move designed to lower global fuel prices ahead of upcoming American midterm elections. Zelenskyy sharply criticized the decision, labeling it weak and warning that it would hand billions of dollars in revenue to Russian President Vladimir Putin, thereby enabling Moscow to intensify its military campaign. In response, an enraged Trump demanded that Kyiv immediately cease targeting Russian oil refineries, even suggesting that Ukraine required a new leader. Zelenskyy countered that leadership choices belong solely to the Ukrainian people, offering to hold elections only if Putin accepted a comprehensive sixty-day ceasefire.

The dispute highlights a growing divergence in strategy between the two nations. Ukraine has increasingly relied on deep drone strikes against Russian oil refineries, supply warehouses, and data centers to weaken Moscow's war economy. Meanwhile, Russian forces have continued relentless aerial bombardments across Ukraine. Recent Russian strikes hit thermal power station number five in Kharkiv, alongside dozens of gas and oil facilities. A brutal attack on Zaporizhzhia claimed twenty-three civilian lives, including four children, while another barrage struck a residential building in Sloviansk. Zelenskyy stressed that any agreement to halt long-range attacks must be reciprocal and backed by concrete security guarantees, including punitive measures against Moscow should it violate the terms.

Behind the scenes, pressure on Kyiv appears to be mounting. Reports indicate that Washington has threatened to halt the procurement system supplying weapons to Ukraine unless deep strikes on Russian soil stop. Furthermore, US negotiators have reportedly explored economic incentives for the Kremlin, such as unfreezing Russian sovereign assets and facilitating multibillion-dollar transactions involving energy giant Lukoil. Ukrainian officials, including foreign affairs committee chairman Oleksandr Merezhko, expressed severe concern, comparing the situation to a modern Molotov-Ribbentrop pact and warning that withholding US intelligence would severely compromise Ukrainian air defenses. Seeking to shore up international support, Zelenskyy held urgent consultations with Western leaders, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who reaffirmed their solidarity and stressed that pressure on Russia must be maintained.

The diplomatic rift underscores the precarious balance between American domestic politics and international security commitments. As energy costs soar globally amid the conflict involving Iran, Washington's focus has increasingly shifted toward market stabilization. However, Ukrainian officials contend that sacrificing Kyiv's strategic leverage without binding commitments from Moscow risks undermining European security. For now, despite Washington's unilateral proclamation, the skies above Ukraine remain contested, with both sides awaiting concrete evidence of whether a genuine energy truce can take hold.

facts.fact: Donald Trump claimed on Truth Social that an 'energy ceasefire' between Russia and Ukraine took effect immediately, though he offered no details.
Volodymyr Zelenskyy said the announced ceasefire deal was 'news to me', though Ukraine supports de-escalation if Russia also stops attacking energy infrastructure.
Trump lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel exports to lower fuel prices before US midterm elections, leading Zelenskyy to call the decision 'weak'.
Trump demanded Ukraine stop attacking Russian oil refineries and suggested Ukraine needed a new leader, to which Zelenskyy responded leadership is up to Ukrainians.
Russian attacks hit Kharkiv thermal power station No 5 and killed 23 people in Zaporizhzhia, including four children.
The US reportedly threatened to halt weapons procurement systems for Ukraine to pressure Kyiv to stop deep strikes inside Russia.
Zelenskyy spoke with international partners, including UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, who reaffirmed support.
